facts.raw_span: left flank pain of 1 week's duration
severe peripheral arterial disease
remote history of ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
percutaneous endovascular stenting of a left popliteal artery aneurysm
well-defined 5 × 12-cm purpuric patch with a darker stellate patch within it
Hematoxylin-eosin stain (×40) showing needle-shaped clefts within the lumen of a blood vessel with minimal perivascular inflammation
eccrine ducts with cellular dyshesion and necrosis
CT of abdomen and pelvis showed no intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal hemorrhages
occluded bilateral common, internal, and external iliac arteries and patent renal arteries
C-reactive protein: 57.50 mg/L
Peripheral eosinophil count, creatinine level, and urinalysis: within normal limits
Urine toxicological screen: negative

concepts.why: The presence of needle-shaped clefts within the lumen of a blood vessel with minimal perivascular inflammation on biopsy, along with occluded bilateral common, internal, and external iliac arteries, supports the diagnosis of cholesterol crystal embolism.
The well-defined purpuric patch with a darker stellate patch within it, along with elevated C-reactive protein, suggests the possibility of vasculitis.

The presence of eccrine ducts with cellular dyshesion and necrosis on biopsy, along with the purpuric patch, could be indicative of caliphylaxis, although the normal creatinine level and urinalysis results make this diagnosis less likely.

The history of percutaneous endovascular stenting of a left popliteal artery aneurysm and the presence of occluded bilateral common, internal, and external iliac arteries could be related to antiphospholipid syndrome, although there is limited direct evidence in the provided facts.
The patient's severe peripheral arterial disease and the findings of occluded iliac arteries are consistent with atherosclerotic peripheral artery disease.
